meaning: The number of descendants from the priestly line of Harim who returned from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 2:39; Nehemiah 7:42). The number has no established symbolic meaning beyond this historical context.
description: The number 1017 appears in the Bible as the count of descendants of Harim who returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile, mentioned in both Ezra 2:39 and Nehemiah 7:42. Harim was a priestly family, and this enumeration is part of the detailed census records documenting the return under Zerubbabel. These lists held great practical and theological significance, as they confirmed lineage and thus the right to serve in the temple. Beyond this specific historical context, the number 1017 has no established symbolic role in biblical numerology or Jewish tradition.

versions.meaning: The number 1017 has no established or known symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: In biblical numerology and Jewish gematria, certain numbers carry strong symbolic significance, such as 7 (perfection), 12 (the tribes of Israel), 40 (testing), and 613 (the number of commandments in the Torah). The number 1017 is not among these and holds no recognized symbolic role in traditional biblical or Jewish texts. It could potentially be analyzed through gematria by finding Hebrew words or phrases with the numerical value 1017, but this does not constitute an established symbolic tradition linked to this number.
versions.reason: [minor] The Description is correct in that 1017 does not have an established symbolic tradition, but it overlooks the fact that the number actually appears in the Bible (Ezra 2:39 and Nehemiah 7:42) as the count of descendants of Harim. This is relevant contextual information that should be mentioned.; [minor] The Meaning field could have been more precise by mentioning the specific biblical occurrence – the number 1017 as the count of descendants of Harim in the return from exile.; [minor] A footnote about the priestly line of Harim and their role in the return from Babylon would provide useful context.

footnotes.text: Harim (חָרִם) is mentioned among the priestly families who could document their genealogy upon returning from Babylon. The name may mean "dedicated" or "curse/ban" (cf. herem), giving it an interesting double meaning in the context of holiness and service.

The population lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are nearly identical but contain some numerical discrepancies for certain families. For the descendants of Harim, the number 1017 is the same in both lists, which strengthens the reliability of the text on this point.

In rabbinic tradition, great emphasis was placed on the accuracy of genealogical records, especially for the priestly lines (kohanim), since only those with verified ancestry could perform temple service (cf. Ezra 2:62–63).
